tasks.routeTitle: Pair each unit with its inverse, leaving ±1
tasks.currentSketch: Pair each unit x modulo n with its inverse. All pairs cancel in the product of units except self-inverse units; in a prime field the only roots of x²=1 are ±1, so (n−1)!≡−1 (mod prime n). This proof applies to prime n (and for composite n the Wilson congruence generally fails).

tasks.entryDescription: Strict descent of remainders; invariant ideals/generated subgroups; continued fractions.
tasks.currentSketch: Repeated division gives a=bq+r with 0≤r<b. Each nonzero remainder is a strictly smaller positive integer, so the process terminates. Since gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,r), the last nonzero remainder is gcd(a,b).

tasks.currentSketch: Among positive elements of I={ax+by:x,y∈Z}, take least d. Division with remainder shows d divides both a and b (otherwise a remainder in I is smaller); every common divisor divides d. So d=gcd(a,b) and lies in (a,b).

tasks.currentSketch: For coprime m,n choose u,v with um+vn=1. Given residues a mod m,b mod n, x=a·vn+b·um has x≡a mod m and x≡b mod n. Any two solutions differ by a multiple of both, hence mn.

tasks.currentSketch: The map φ:Z/(mn)→Z/m×Z/n sending a residue to its pair of residues is a ring homomorphism. Its kernel is multiples of mn, hence trivial; finite sets have equal size mn, so it is an isomorphism.

tasks.entryDescription: Construct coefficients with Bezout identities; ring isomorphism via kernels/ideals; Lagrange interpolation/idempotents.
tasks.currentSketch: For pairwise coprime moduli n₁,…,nₖ, put N=∏nᵢ and Nⱼ=N/nⱼ. Choose yⱼ with Nⱼyⱼ≡1 (mod nⱼ), and set x=Σⱼ bⱼNⱼyⱼ. Modulo nᵢ, every summand except the i-th vanishes and the i-th is bᵢ, giving all required congruences. If x and x′ are two solutions, every nⱼ divides x−x′; pairwise coprimality implies N divides x−x′, proving uniqueness modulo N.

tasks.entryDescription: Triangulation and induction; boundary/interior lattice-point counting plus Euler characteristic; reduce to unimodular triangles.
tasks.currentSketch: Triangulate a lattice polygon into lattice triangles and prove the formula inductively by adding triangles along edges; boundary lattice points and interior lattice points update exactly as the area does. A primitive lattice triangle (no lattice points except vertices) has area 1/2 by the determinant/unimodular lemma. The resulting invariant is A=I+B/2−1.

tasks.routeTitle: boundary/interior lattice-point counting plus Euler characteristic
tasks.currentSketch: For a lattice triangulation, each triangle has area equal to its number of interior lattice points plus half its boundary count minus 1 (Pick's formula for a triangle, via determinant/lattice-index argument). Sum over triangles; interior edges are counted twice and vertices satisfy Euler's planar formula, leaving A=I+B/2−1.

tasks.currentSketch: Repeatedly subdivide a lattice polygon using an interior or boundary lattice point until all pieces are primitive lattice triangles. Each primitive triangle has area 1/2; counting how pieces meet and using Euler characteristic gives A=I+B/2−1. The primitive-triangle claim is essential and follows from lattice index / determinant.
